items.title: The earliest Christians thought Jesus would return within their lifetime
items.claim: Paul's letters (50s CE) are the oldest Christian texts. What does he tell his churches about the timing of Christ's return?

options.text: He explicitly warns that it will be many centuries away
He tells believers — in 1 Thessalonians 4 and 1 Corinthians 15 — that 'we who are alive, who are left' will be caught up to meet the Lord
He refuses to discuss the timing at all
He places the return precisely at AD 70, the destruction of the Temple

items.reveal:
1 Thessalonians 4:15-17, written around 50-51 CE, includes Paul among those still alive at the Parousia. 1 Corinthians 7:29 says 'the appointed time has grown short.' Mark 9:1 has Jesus saying 'some standing here will not taste death' before seeing the Kingdom.

When Christ did not return, later texts (e.g. 2 Peter 3:8 — 'one day is with the Lord as a thousand years') reinterpret the delay. This shift is one of the central transformations of early Christian theology.
items.why: Treating the New Testament as a unified, settled doctrine misses that it documents a community reinterpreting itself in real time. The 'delay of the Parousia' is one of the formative pressures on Christian thought.

items.title: The Torah is the first five books of the Hebrew Bible

options.text: The first five books — Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy — traditionally attributed to Moses; also called the Pentateuch or Chumash; the first section of the Hebrew Bible (Tanakh)

items.reveal:
The Hebrew Bible (Tanakh) is structured in three sections: Torah (Teaching, 5 books), Nevi'im (Prophets, 8 books in Jewish count), Ketuvim (Writings, 11 books). 'Tanakh' is an acronym of those three.

The Torah is read in synagogue in an annual cycle (some Reform congregations use a triennial cycle). The cycle ends and restarts on Simchat Torah.

The Written Torah is complemented by the Oral Torah — the rabbinic tradition codified in the Mishnah (around 200 CE) and Talmud (around 500 CE). For Orthodox Judaism, both were revealed at Sinai.
items.why: 'The Torah' is often used loosely. Students need to distinguish Torah (5 books) from Tanakh (24 books) from Talmud (rabbinic commentary) — and notice that the Christian Old Testament has the same content but in different order.

items.title: Act and rule utilitarianism produce different answers
items.claim: What is the act-rule distinction in utilitarianism?

options.text: Act utilitarianism judges each action by its direct consequences; rule utilitarianism asks which rules, if generally followed, would maximise utility — and applies those rules even when an individual act might seem to give a different answer
Act utilitarianism is the only legitimate form

items.reveal:
Jeremy Bentham's 'Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation' (1789) introduced the hedonic calculus. John Stuart Mill's 'Utilitarianism' (1861) distinguished higher and lower pleasures.

Rule utilitarianism (developed by R. M. Hare and Richard Brandt in the 20th century) attempts to address objections to act utilitarianism — that it permits horrific acts (killing one innocent to save five) and creates impossible decision burdens.

Critics argue rule utilitarianism collapses into act utilitarianism (just add 'except in special cases') or into Kantian deontology (just follow the rules).
items.why: Utilitarianism is not one theory. The act/rule distinction changes the answers radically — and exam answers that treat 'utilitarianism' as monolithic miss the most important internal debate.
